title: Risk and Adaptivity in Certifying Machine-Learning Model Comparisons
abstract:
Background. When verification records are incomplete, an auditor needs to know whether further readings will make a model comparison precise enough. We ask when choosing the next reading after seeing an earlier answer improves that guarantee under a fixed budget.

Methods. We bound model-loss differences over all compatible records. We classify scalar width penalties and prove a shared-query separation with matching lower bounds. We then check precision certificates on frozen forecast comparisons and replay the policies on stored answers.

Results. A shared-query construction has optimal adaptive mean joint width 1/2, versus 2/3 for randomized batching, with matching lower bounds. For scalar width, the two minimax risks agree universally exactly for nondecreasing concave penalties. On 165 of 819 original blocks and 57 of 279 external blocks, two shared adaptive readings guarantee joint half-width precision, whereas optimal randomized-batch worst-case success is exactly 50%. These are precision-success guarantees, distinct from mean-width risk. On the certified subsets, recorded success is 100% versus 65.45% and 64.91% for the selected optimal batch mixtures. Complete-panel replay gives 7.81- and 11.11-percentage-point gains over fixed worst-width batches, and 2.20- and 2.15-point gains over greedy adaptation. Under illustrative 1% internal errors with exact endpoints, 45 external blocks retain an adaptive guarantee that every randomized batch fails to match. Capacity information reduces this advantage, and measured public-API retrieval favors bulk.

Conclusions. These guarantees depend on the supplied bounds and access rules. The shared-budget evidence is retrospective; physical meter accuracy and improved downstream model choice are not established.
